claim: SBT5.2 is a serine protease of the subtilase family that was identified as a MYB30-interacting partner in a yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: In order to search for components involved in MYB30-mediated signalling, a Y2H screen was previously conducted using a MYB30 version deleted from its transcriptional activation domain (MYB30ΔAD) (Froidure et al., 2010) as bait. A cDNA clone encoding the last 103 amino acids of the Arabidopsis serine protease of the subtilisin group SBT5.2 (At1g20160) was identified in this screen (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the Y2H screen methodology and the identification of SBT5.2 as an interacting partner, with reference to Figure 1 showing the interaction results.

claim: SBT5.2 belongs to subgroup V within the classification of the Arabidopsis subtilase family.
source: SBT5.2 belongs to subgroup V (6 members) within the classification of the Arabidopsis subtilase family (Schaller et al., 2012; Rautengarten et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with citations to previous classification studies.

claim: The SBT5.2 gene produces two distinct transcripts through alternative splicing.
source: Two gene models are annotated in the TAIR database (http://www.arabidopsis.org) for At1g20160, suggesting that the corresponding transcript is alternatively spliced (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by database annotation and confirmed by Figure 2a showing the genomic structure of the two splice variants.

claim: The first intron is specifically spliced in the SBT5.2(b) cDNA but retained in SBT5.2(a).
source: Comparison of the two SBT5.2 cDNA clones [designated SBT5.2(a) and SBT5.2(b)] with the genomic sequence revealed that the first intron is specifically spliced in the SBT5.2(b) cDNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Both SBT5.2 splice variants exist in planta as confirmed by RT-PCR.
source: Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) using specific cDNA primers confirmed the existence of both splice variants in planta (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Expression of SBT5.2(a) is downregulated after bacterial inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1.
source: As shown in Figure 2c, expression of SBT5.2(a) was downregulated after treatment with bacteria, whereas expression of SBT5.2(b) was induced and displayed an expression profile highly similar to that of MYB30 (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2c following bacterial inoculation.

claim: Expression of SBT5.2(b) is induced after bacterial inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1.
source: As shown in Figure 2c, expression of SBT5.2(a) was downregulated after treatment with bacteria, whereas expression of SBT5.2(b) was induced and displayed an expression profile highly similar to that of MYB30 (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2c following bacterial inoculation.

claim: SBT5.2(b) expression profile is highly similar to that of MYB30 after bacterial treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 2c, expression of SBT5.2(a) was downregulated after treatment with bacteria, whereas expression of SBT5.2(b) was induced and displayed an expression profile highly similar to that of MYB30 (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: SBT5.2(a) corresponds to a transcript of 2402 bp encoding a 769 amino acid preproenzyme.
source: SBT5.2(a) corresponds to a transcript of 2402 bp, which is predicted to encode a 769 amino acid preproenzyme containing a signal peptide (SP) followed a by prodomain (PD), which acts as an intramolecular inhibitor, and a mature polypeptide (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SBT5.2(a) contains a signal peptide followed by a prodomain.
source: SBT5.2(a) corresponds to a transcript of 2402 bp, which is predicted to encode a 769 amino acid preproenzyme containing a signal peptide (SP) followed a by prodomain (PD), which acts as an intramolecular inhibitor, and a mature polypeptide (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure prediction shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SBT5.2(b) corresponds to a transcript of 2373 bp encoding a protein of 730 amino acids.
source: In contrast, SBT5.2(b) corresponds to a transcript of 2373 bp, predicted to encode a protein of 730 amino acids with no SP and lacking the first five amino acids of the PD (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SBT5.2(b) lacks a signal peptide and the first five amino acids of the prodomain.
source: In contrast, SBT5.2(b) corresponds to a transcript of 2373 bp, predicted to encode a protein of 730 amino acids with no SP and lacking the first five amino acids of the PD (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure analysis shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both SBT5.2 proteins contain a catalytic triad with three conserved amino acids (D145, H210 and S546 in SBT5.2(a), and D106, H171 and S507 in SBT5.2(b)).
source: Except for their N-terminal differences, the two corresponding encoded proteins are predicted to be identical and contain a catalytic triad with three amino acids (D145, H210 and S546 in SBT5.2(a), and D106, H171 and S507 in SBT5.2(b)) conserved within serine proteases (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis showing conserved catalytic residues in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: SBT5.2(a) is located in apoplastic spaces.
source: As expected, SBT5.2(a) was found to be located in apoplastic spaces whereas SBT5.2(b) was detected at vesicle-like structures inside cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: SBT5.2(b) is detected at vesicle-like structures inside cells.
source: As expected, SBT5.2(a) was found to be located in apoplastic spaces whereas SBT5.2(b) was detected at vesicle-like structures inside cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: SBT5.2(a) is secreted to the intercellular fluid.
source: SBT5.2(a) was detected in the IF as two protein bands that may correspond to the processed and unprocessed forms of the protease, whereas SBT5.2(b) was exclusively detected in the TE and never in the IF fraction (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: SBT5.2(b) is exclusively intracellular and not secreted.
source: SBT5.2(a) was detected in the IF as two protein bands that may correspond to the processed and unprocessed forms of the protease, whereas SBT5.2(b) was exclusively detected in the TE and never in the IF fraction (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Secretion of SBT5.2(a) was previously reported.
source: Indeed, secretion of SBT5.2(a) was previously reported (Engineer et al., 2014; Kaschani et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Seven putative N-linked glycosylation sites are present in SBT5.2 proteins.
source: Seven putative N-linked glycosylation sites (PGSs; N in NxS/T motifs) are present in SBT5.2 proteins [N225, N363, N467, N525, N636, N650 and N678 in SBT5.2(a)].
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis identifying N-glycosylation motifs.

claim: SBT5.2(a) is N-glycosylated in planta.
source: Finally, the increased electrophoretic mobility of SBT5.2(a) in protein extracts from N. benthamiana leaves expressing HA-tagged SBT5.2(a) and treated with tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation of newly synthesized glycoproteins in the ER (Bassik and Kampmann, 2011), further confirmed SBT5.2(a) N-glycosylation in planta (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by tunicamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 3c, as well as PNGase F/EndoH treatment and concanavalin A binding assays.

claim: All seven putative glycosylation sites in SBT5.2(a) are used in planta.
source: This analysis revealed a small but significant mobility shift for all SBT5.2(a) PGS mutants (Figure 3d), suggesting that all PGS in SBT5.2(a) are used in planta.
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis and electrophoretic mobility analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: SBT5.2(b) is not N-glycosylated.
source: Despite the fact that SBT5.2(b) contains the seven PGSs present in SBT5.2(a), (i) SBT5.2(b) electrophoretic mobility was not modified after treatment with PNGase F or EndoH (Figure 3a); (ii) neither SBT5.2(b) binding to nor elution from a concanavalin A resin was observed (Figure 3b); and (iii) no effect of tunicamycin leaf treatment on the SBT5.2(b) electrophoresis profile was detected (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple biochemical assays shown in Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c.

claim: SBT5.2(b) does not enter the secretory pathway.
source: These results, which are consistent with the absence of SP in SBT5.2(b) and our previous observation that SBT5.2(b) is not secreted, strongly suggest that SBT5.2(b) does not enter the secretory pathway and is therefore not N-glycosylated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of glycosylation and secretion data, combined with the absence of a signal peptide.

claim: SBT5.2(a) is able to auto-process in planta.
source: This observation suggests that SBT5.2(a) is able to auto-process in planta and is thus active as a protease.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mutation of the catalytic histidine prevents processing, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: SBT5.2(b) does not self-process in planta.
source: Following transient expression in N. benthamiana, mutation of the catalytic histidine residue did not affect migration of SBT5.2(b) as compared to the wild-type protein, suggesting that this protein does not self-process in planta (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: SBT5.2(a) displays protease activity.
source: Increased fluorescence was observed for SBT5.2(a), reflecting proteolytic cleavage of the FITC-casein substrate (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorimetric protease activity assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: SBT5.2(b) does not display protease activity.
source: In contrast, fluorescence intensity in the case of SBT5.2(a)H210A, SBT5.2(b) and SBT5.2(b)H171A was indistinguishable from that of protoplasts transformed with an empty vector (Figure 4b), although their protein expression levels were comparable to those of SBT5.2(a) (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorimetric protease activity assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neither SBT5.2(a) nor SBT5.2(b) proteolytically cleave MYB30.
source: As shown in Figure 4c, MYB30 accumulation was consistently unaltered in the presence of SBT5.2(a) or SBT5.2(b) as compared to the expression observed in the presence of the respective subtilase catalytic mutant versions. These results suggest that neither SBT5.2(a) nor SBT5.2(b) are able to proteolytically cleave MYB30.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of MYB30 accumulation shown in Figure 4c.

claim: SBT5.2(a) and MYB30 do not colocalize in planta.
source: Confocal microscopy analysis of N. benthamiana leaves transiently co-expressing GFP-MYB30 and SBT5.2(a)-RFP showed that these proteins do not co-localize in planta, as SBT5.2(a) and MYB30 retain their respective extracellular and nuclear localization when expressed together (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: SBT5.2(b) causes nuclear exclusion of MYB30 when co-expressed.
source: Surprisingly, when co-expressed with RFP-tagged SBT5.2(b), GFP-MYB30 was excluded from the nucleus and localized to the same vesicle-like structures where SBT5.2(b) was localized, suggesting a possible in planta interaction between the two proteins outside the nucleus (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: SBT5.2(b)-mediated nuclear exclusion of MYB30 is specific.
source: Importantly, the unrelated MYB TF MYB123 retained its nuclear localization when co-expressed with SBT5.2(b), suggesting that SBT5.2(b)-mediated MYB30 nuclear exclusion is specific (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing MYB123 localization in Figure 5a.

claim: SBT5.2(b)-mediated nuclear exclusion of MYB30 is confirmed in Arabidopsis protoplasts.
source: Moreover, SBT5.2(b)-mediated specific nuclear exclusion of MYB30 was confirmed in Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data in Arabidopsis protoplasts shown in Figure 5b.

claim: MYB30 physically interacts with SBT5.2(b) in intracellular vesicles.
source: A significant reduction of GFP lifetime was observed when GFP-MYB30 was co-expressed with RFP-tagged SBT5.2(b) as compared to co-expression with SBT5.2(b)-HA, both in N. benthamiana epidermal cells and in Arabidopsis protoplasts, thus confirming the physical interaction between the two proteins in intracellular vesicles (Figure 5c,d; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 5c, 5d, and Table 1.

claim: The interaction between MYB30 and SBT5.2(b) does not depend on the integrity of SBT5.2(b) catalytic triad.
source: This interaction did not depend on the integrity of SBT5.2(b) catalytic triad, as shown by the reduced GFP lifetime of GFP-MYB30 when co-expressed with RFP-tagged SBT5.2(b)H171A (Table 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET-FLIM data with catalytic mutant shown in Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The C-terminus of SBT5.2(b) is sufficient for interaction with MYB30.
source: A significant reduction of the average GFP lifetime was measured in nuclei coexpressing GFP-MYB30 and SBT5.2(b)362-730-RFP, as compared to nuclei expressing GFP-MYB30 alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d; Table 1), confirming that the C-terminus of SBT5.2(b) is sufficient for the interaction with MYB30.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET-FLIM data with truncated SBT5.2(b) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d and Table 1.

claim: The C-terminal domain of SBT5.1 does not interact with MYB30.
source: The specificity of this observation was highlighted by the lack of interaction between GFP-MYB30 and the equivalent C-terminal domain of the closest Arabidopsis SBT5.2 homolog, SBT5.1, (SBT5.1405-780-RFP) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b,e; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET-FLIM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b, 2e, and Table 1.

claim: SBT5.2(b) localizes to trans-Golgi network/early endosomes (TGN/EE).
source: Colocalization with of SBT5.2(b) with these endosomal markers was clearly observed in N. benthamiana leaves (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization with VHA-a1 and SYP61 markers shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SBT5.2(b) localizes to late endosomes/multivesicular bodies (LE/MVB).
source: Colocalization with of SBT5.2(b) with these endosomal markers was clearly observed in N. benthamiana leaves (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization with ARA6 and SYP21 markers shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SBT5.2(b) does not colocalize with the Golgi marker GmMan-GFP.
source: In contrast, no colocalization of SBT5.2(b)-RFP with the Golgi marker GmMan-GFP (Nelson et al., 2007) was detected (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: A free N-terminal myristoylation site in SBT5.2(b) is necessary for its endosomal targeting.
source: Together, our data strongly suggest that a free N-terminal myristoylated residue is responsible of SBT5.2(b) targeting to the endosomes and of MYB30 retention in endosomal vesicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis and localization data showing that N-terminal modifications prevent endosomal localization, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Mutation of the putatively myristoylated Gly2 residue to Ala in SBT5.2(b) results in cytoplasmic localization.
source: A SBT5.2(b) version in which the putatively myristoylated Gly2 residue was mutated to Ala [SBT5.2(b)G2A] also localized to the cytoplasm (Figure 6b), confirming the importance of N-myristoylation for SBT5.2(b) endosomal targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data of the G2A mutant shown in Figure 6b.

claim: SBT5.2(b) interferes with endosomal trafficking, causing colocalization of early and late endosome markers.
source: In contrast, co-expression with SBT5.2(b) led to co-localization of VHA-a1 and ARA6 in the same endosomal compartment, strongly suggesting that SBT5.2(b) is able to interfere with endosomal trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization of normally distinct endosomal markers in Figure 7.

claim: Myristoylation of SBT5.2(b) is essential for its effect on endosomal trafficking.
source: Myristoylation of SBT5.2(b) appears to be essential to this effect, since expression of SBT5.2(b)G2A did not affect the discrete endosomal populations tagged by VHA-a1 or ARA6 (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data with the G2A mutant shown in Figure 7.

claim: sbt5.2 mutant plants show stronger HR cell death symptoms after inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1 compared to wild-type plants.
source: Similar to MYB30-overexpressing (MYB30OE), sbt5.2 mutant plants showed stronger HR cell death symptoms after inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1 as compared to Col-0 wild-type plants (Figure 8a).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual symptoms and ion leakage measurements shown in Figure 8a and 8b.

claim: sbt5.2 mutant plants display increased resistance to Pst AvrRpm1 compared to wild-type plants.
source: In agreement with faster HR development, sbt5.2 plants showed increased resistance in response to inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1, as compared to wild-type plants (Figure 8c), confirming the role of SBT5.2 as a negative regulator of plant defence.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth assays shown in Figure 8c.

claim: SBT5.2 acts as a negative regulator of plant defence.
source: In agreement with faster HR development, sbt5.2 plants showed increased resistance in response to inoculation with Pst AvrRpm1, as compared to wild-type plants (Figure 8c), confirming the role of SBT5.2 as a negative regulator of plant defence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced defence phenotype of sbt5.2 mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: sbt5.2 mutant plants display higher expression of MYB30 target genes FDH and CER2 compared to wild-type plants after bacterial inoculation.
source: Importantly, sbt5.2 mutant plants displayed higher expression of MYB30 VLCFA-related target genes FDH and CER2 (Raffaele et al., 2008) as compared to Col-0 wild-type plants 1 hr after inoculation (Figure 9a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR gene expression data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: The enhanced expression of MYB30 target genes in sbt5.2 mutants is abolished in the myb30 mutant background.
source: Moreover, this phenotype was abolished in the myb30 mutant background (sbt5.2 myb30; Figure 9a) and correlated with loss of increased HR in the sbt5.2 myb30 double mutant (Figure 9b).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data in double mutants shown in Figure 9a.

claim: The increased HR phenotype of sbt5.2 mutants is lost in the sbt5.2 myb30 double mutant.
source: Moreover, this phenotype was abolished in the myb30 mutant background (sbt5.2 myb30; Figure 9a) and correlated with loss of increased HR in the sbt5.2 myb30 double mutant (Figure 9b).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death measurements in double mutants shown in Figure 9b.

claim: SBT5.2 negatively regulates Arabidopsis defence through repression of MYB30 transcriptional activity.
source: Together, these data confirm that SBT5.2 negatively regulates Arabidopsis defence through repression of MYB30 transcriptional activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic epistasis experiments showing MYB30-dependence of sbt5.2 phenotypes.

claim: Overexpression of SBT5.2(b), but not SBT5.2(a), suppresses the increased HR phenotype of sbt5.2 mutants.
source: Importantly, the increased HR phenotype displayed by the sbt5.2 mutant was specifically suppressed in sbt5.2 plants overexpressing SBT5.2(b), but not SBT5.2(a) (Figure 9c).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death measurements in complementation lines shown in Figure 9c.

claim: Overexpression of SBT5.2(b), but not SBT5.2(a), suppresses enhanced accumulation of phenolic compounds in sbt5.2 mutants.
source: Enhanced accumulation of phenolic compounds, characteristic of HR cell death, was detected in MYB30OE ans sbt5.2 mutant lines as compared to wild-type Col-0 and this phenotype was suppressed both in sbt5.2 myb30 double mutants and by overexpressing SBT5.2(b), but not SBT5.2(a), in the sbt5.2 mutant background (Figure 9d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenolic compound accumulation data shown in Figure 9d and 9e.

claim: Negative regulation of MYB30-mediated defence-related cell death is specifically controlled by SBT5.2(b).
source: Overall our data demonstrate that, in agreement with SBT5.2(b)-mediated retention of MYB30 in endosomes, negative regulation of MYB30-mediated defence-related cell death is specifically controlled by SBT5.2(b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the complementation experiments showing specific rescue by SBT5.2(b).

claim: Alternative splicing of SBT5.2 represents the first described example of AS affecting the function of a protein of the subtilase family.
source: To our knowledge, our work represents the first described example of AS affecting the function of a protein of the subtilase family.
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Alternative splicing plays fundamental roles in regulating plant growth, development, and responses to environmental signals.
source: In plants, AS plays fundamental roles in regulating plant growth, development, and responses to environmental signals (Staiger and Brown, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: A genome-wide transcriptomic analysis in Arabidopsis plants inoculated with bacteria uncovered a large number of AS events.
source: A genome-wide transcriptomic analysis in Arabidopsis plants inoculated with bacteria uncovered a surprisingly large number of AS events (Howard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The function of numerous plant resistance genes encoding immune receptors appears to be regulated by alternative splicing.
source: Although we are still far from understanding the functional implications of this transcriptome complexity, the function of numerous plant resistance genes, encoding immune receptors, appears to be regulated by AS (Yang et al., 2014; Gassmann, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Plant subtilases are usually synthesized as preproprotein precursors with an N-terminal ER-targeting signal peptide.
source: Plant subtilases are usually synthesized in the form of preproprotein precursors, translocated via an N-terminal ER-targeting SP into the endomembrane system (Schaller et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Plant subtilases are glycosylated in the secretory pathway and accumulate extracellularly.
source: In addition, using mass spectrometry (Cedzich et al., 2009) and structural analyses (Murayama et al., 2012), plant subtilases were shown to be glycosylated in the secretory pathway and to accumulate extracellularly (Schaller et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The prodomain of plant subtilases acts as an auto-inhibitor domain.
source: Processing of the PD, an auto-inhibitor domain of plant subtilases (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2016), is an intramolecular autocatalytic reaction that occurs late in the ER or in the early Golgi (Cedzich et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SBT5.2 was previously described as a negative regulator of stomatal density under high CO2 conditions through cleavage of the extracellular pro-peptide ligand EPF2.
source: SBT5.2 was previously described as a negative regulator of stomatal density under high CO2 conditions through cleavage of the extracellular pro-peptide ligand EPF2 in the apoplast (Engineer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Examples of proteases playing proteolysis-independent functions have been described in mammals.
source: Examples of proteases playing proteolysis-independent functions have been described in mammals.
evidence: The claim is supported by subsequent examples of PCSK9 and γ-secretase.

claim: The proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) does not require its catalytic activity to induce degradation of low-density lipoproteins.
source: The proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) plays a major regulatory role in cholesterol homeostasis but does not require its catalytic activity to induce degradation of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) (McNutt et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: γ-secretase displays proteolysis-independent functions during the regulation of βAPP maturation and trafficking.
source: In addition, γ-secretase, an aspartyl protease that performs the final proteolytic cleavage step in the processing cascade of the β-amyloid precursor protein (βAPP) (Vassar et al., 1999), displays proteolysis-independent functions during the regulation of βAPP maturation and trafficking (Wrigley et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active Rab5 in mammals blocks the conversion of early to late endosomes, giving rise to hybrid endosomal compartments.
source: In mammals, expression of constitutively active Rab5 blocks the conversion of early to late endosomes, giving rise to hybrid endosomal compartments and deregulation of autophagy (Rink et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Overexpression of Arabidopsis sorting nexin SNX2b leads to the formation of large SNX2-containing endosome aggregations, which inhibits vesicle trafficking.
source: Similarly, overexpression of Arabidopsis sorting nexin SNX2b leads to the formation of large SNX2-containing endosome aggregations, which inhibits vesicle trafficking (Phan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Endosomal trafficking pathways control multiple signalling pathways, including those involved in plant disease resistance.
source: SBT5.2(b)-mediated regulation of MYB30 activity supports the emerging idea that endosomal trafficking pathways are not only central regulators of plasma membrane protein homeostasis but also control multiple signalling pathways, including those involved in plant disease resistance (Reyes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Enhanced susceptibility of plants impaired in regulators of endosome trafficking emphasizes the importance of endocytic processes in establishing defence.
source: Enhanced susceptibility of plants impaired in regulators of endosome trafficking emphasizes the importance of endocytic processes in establishing defence (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Plasma membrane receptors that sense apoplastic microbes are immune-related cargos of plant trafficking pathways.
source: In addition, plasma membrane receptors that sense apoplastic microbes are immune-related cargos of plant trafficking pathways (Beck et al., 2012; Ben Khaled et al., 2015), and a number of intracellular immune receptors have been shown to constitutively localize to endomembranes (Takemoto et al., 2012; Engelhardt et al., 2012), further underlining the prominent role of endomembrane systems in determining plant resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Relocalisation of the potato resistance protein R3a from the cytoplasm to endosomal compartments is required to trigger the HR.
source: Indeed, relocalisation of the potato resistance protein R3a from the cytoplasm to endosomal compartments is required to trigger the HR (Engelhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The bacterial effector HopM1 targets and degrades the Arabidopsis ARF-GEF MIN7, altering secretory trafficking.
source: For example, the Arabidopsis ADP ribosylation factor (ARF)-Guanine exchange factor (GEF) MIN7 is targeted and degraded by the bacterial effector HopM1 altering secretory trafficking (Nomura et al., 2006, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effector PipB2 from Salmonella enterica causes redistribution of late endosomes/lysosomes compartments to the cell periphery.
source: In mammalian cells, the effector PipB2 from the bacterial pathogen Salmonella enterica causes a specific redistribution of late endosomes/lysosomes (LE/Lys) compartments to the cell periphery promoting formation of Salmonella-induced filaments (Sifs) (Knodler and Steele-Mortimer, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Subcellular compartmentalization of the E2F TF family is used to control cell cycle in differentiated skeletal cells.
source: Subcellular compartmentalization of the E2F TF family, either in the nucleus or in the cytoplasm, is used to control cell cycle in differentiated skeletal cells (Gill and Hamel, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: p53 shifts from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in the presence of HDM2, where it has important roles independent of its transcriptional activity.
source: p53, a tightly regulated animal TF that acts as a hub for numerous signalling pathways including apoptosis, shifts from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in the presence of HDM2, where it has important roles that are independent of its transcriptional activity (Boyd et al., 2000; Green and Kroemer, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Arabidopsis SBT6.1 cleaves the ER-located TF bZIP17, which then moves to the nucleus to activate transcription in response to salt stress.
source: Arabidopsis SBT6.1 is able to cleave the ER-located TF bZIP17 that, once released, moves to the nucleus to activate transcription in response to salt stress (Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The small interference protein MIF1 promotes nuclear exclusion of the TF ZHD5 by relocalizing it to cytoplasmic vesicle-like structures.
source: Indeed, the small interference protein MIF1, promotes nuclear exclusion of the TF ZHD5 that regulates flower architecture and leaf development. As a result, ZHD5 is relocalised into cytoplasmic vesicle-like structures, which interferes with is transcriptional activity (Hong et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MYB30 is regulated by the secreted phospholipase AtsPLA2-α through nuclear relocalization.
source: During the last few years, different regulatory mechanisms of MYB30-mediated HR have been uncovered (Raffaele and Rivas, 2013), including spatio-temporal control of MYB30 activity through the action of the secreted phospholipase AtsPLA2-α (that specifically relocalises to the nucleus in the presence of MYB30 [Froidure et al., 2010]) and the RING-type E3 ligase MIEL1 (that ubiquitinates MYB30 and leads to its proteasomal degradation [Marino et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MYB30 is regulated by the RING-type E3 ligase MIEL1 through ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: During the last few years, different regulatory mechanisms of MYB30-mediated HR have been uncovered (Raffaele and Rivas, 2013), including spatio-temporal control of MYB30 activity through the action of the secreted phospholipase AtsPLA2-α (that specifically relocalises to the nucleus in the presence of MYB30 [Froidure et al., 2010]) and the RING-type E3 ligase MIEL1 (that ubiquitinates MYB30 and leads to its proteasomal degradation [Marino et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SBT5.2(b)-mediated nuclear exclusion of MYB30 represents an additional regulatory mode of MYB30 transcription factor activity.
source: SBT5.2(b)-mediated nuclear exclusion of MYB30 represents an additional regulatory mode of the activity of this TF, underlining the complexity of the regulatory modes of defence-related plant cell death responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the novel mechanism described in this study in the context of previously known regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The intricate regulation of MYB30 is reminiscent of the tight control exerted on animal TFs such as p53.
source: This intricate regulation of MYB30 is reminiscent of the tight control exerted on animal TFs such as p53 that is also multi-regulated through varied modes including protein-protein interactions, ubiquitination and, notably, nuclear exclusion.
evidence: The claim is a comparison drawn by the authors based on knowledge of p53 regulation.

claim: Sophisticated fine-tuning of transcription factor activity provides an efficient means to regulate fundamental cellular processes and appears as a general feature underlying transcriptional control in eukaryotic cells.
source: This sophisticated fine-tuning, which provides an efficient means to regulate fundamental cellular processes, appears as a general feature underlying the transcriptional control in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: The claim is a general conclusion drawn by the authors based on the findings and comparison with other systems.

claim: Subtilases belong to the S8 family within the SB clan of serine proteases.
source: According to the MEROPS (http://merops.sanger.ac.uk) classification, subtilases belong to the S8 family within the SB clan of serine proteases and are grouped into two subfamilies, subtilisins (S8A) and kexins (S8B).
evidence: The claim is based on established classification from the MEROPS database.

claim: Nine subtilases have been characterized in mammals, seven of which belong to the kexin group.
source: Nine subtilases have been characterized in mammals, seven of which belong to the kexin group and two others to the S8A subfamily (pyrolysins).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about mammalian subtilases.

claim: Plant subtilases exclusively belong to the pyrolysin group within the S8A subfamily with no representatives of the kexin type.
source: With no representatives of the kexin type, plant subtilases exclusively belong to the pyrolysin group within the S8A subfamily.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about plant subtilases.

claim: In Arabidopsis the subtilase family comprises 56 members distributed in six distinct subgroups (SBT1-6).
source: In Arabidopsis the subtilase family comprises 56 members distributed in six distinct subgroups (SBT1-6) (Rautengarten et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous classification study.

claim: Subtilases have been involved in general protein turnover as well as in the highly specific regulation of plant development or responses to environmental changes.
source: Subtilases are predicted to be secreted and have been involved in general protein turnover as well as in the highly specific regulation of plant development or responses to environmental changes and, more recently, in suppression of basal immunity and immune priming (Schaller et al., 2012; Figueiredo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Subtilases have been involved in suppression of basal immunity and immune priming.
source: Subtilases are predicted to be secreted and have been involved in general protein turnover as well as in the highly specific regulation of plant development or responses to environmental changes and, more recently, in suppression of basal immunity and immune priming (Schaller et al., 2012; Figueiredo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Plants lack mobile defender cells and a somatic adaptive immune system.
source: Plants, unlike mammals, lack mobile defender cells and a somatic adaptive immune system.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about plant immunity.

claim: Plants rely on the innate immunity of each cell and on systemic signals originating from infection sites.
source: Instead, they rely on the innate immunity of each cell and on systemic signals originating from infection sites.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about plant immunity.

claim: Plant resistance to disease is often associated with the hypersensitive response (HR), a form of programmed cell death.
source: Plant resistance to disease is a costly response, closely connected to plant physiological and developmental processes, and often associated with the so-called hypersensitive response (HR), a form of programmed cell death that develops at attempted infection sites, allegedly to prevent pathogen propagation through the plant (Coll et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MYB30 is one of the best characterized MYB TFs regulating defence-related transcription in Arabidopsis.
source: Among the MYB TFs regulating defence-related transcription, Arabidopsis MYB30 is one of the best characterized.
evidence: The claim is stated based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: MYB30 promotes defence and cell death-associated responses through transcriptional activation of genes related to the lipid biosynthesis pathway leading to production of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs).
source: MYB30 promotes defence and cell death-associated responses through the transcriptional activation of genes related to the lipid biosynthesis pathway that leads to the production of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) (Raffaele et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: MYB30 is targeted by the effector protein XopD from Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, leading to suppression of MYB30-mediated transcriptional activation of plant resistance.
source: MYB30 is targeted by the effector protein XopD, from the bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris (Xcc), leading to suppression of MYB30-mediated transcriptional activation of plant resistance and thus underlining the important role played by MYB30 in plant defence regulation (Canonne et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Co-expression of MYB30ΔAD and SBT5.2628-730 resulted in yeast growth on selective medium.
source: Co-expression of MYB30 deleted from its C-terminal transcription activation domain (MYB30△AD) and the isolated cDNA clone encoding the last 103 amino acids of SBT5.2 (SBT5.2628-730) resulted in yeast growth on selective medium.
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Yeast cells expressing MYB30ΔAD or SBT5.2628-730 with control proteins were not able to grow on selective medium.
source: In a control experiment, yeast cells expressing MYB30△AD or SBT5.2628-730 with controls provided by Clontech (T-antigen or P53, respectively) were not able to grow on selective medium.
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 1.
